title: Best Field Service Software for a One-Truck Shop
meta: One truck, one phone, no office. You don't need an enterprise platform — you need simple that works. Why Jobber fits most solo shops, and who should wait.
short: You don't need the enterprise stuff. For most one-truck shops, keep it simple — and that usually means Jobber.
statLabel: A solo shop needs the boring core done well, not fifty features you'll never open

body.answer: A one-truck shop should buy the simplest tool that nails scheduling, quoting and payment — not the one with the most features.
body.html:
You run the truck, answer the phone, do the work, and send the invoice. You are the whole company. The last thing you need is software built for a 40-tech operation with a dispatch room. You need the boring core done well, scheduling, quoting, invoicing, getting paid, and nothing fighting you for attention.

So let's skip the part where we pretend every tool is equally right for you. For most one-truck shops, the answer is Jobber, and we'll tell you exactly why, plus who should ignore that advice.

body.h2: Why Jobber fits most solo operators
body.answer: Jobber does the solo-shop essentials cleanly and is easy to learn, which is exactly what one person running everything needs.
body.html:
When you're a one-person show, the tax isn't the monthly fee, it's the time to learn and run the thing. Jobber keeps that tax low. The core flow is obvious, the mobile app is built for someone standing in a driveway, and you're not paying for dispatch-board features you'll never touch. That's the whole game for a solo operator: low friction, does the essentials, stays out of your way.

We lay out the strengths and the honest gripes in the Jobber review. Check current pricing there, it moves, so we're not quoting a number that'll be wrong next quarter.

The other reason it fits solo operators: it grows with you without forcing a migration the day you hire your first helper. You can start on the lowest plan, running everything yourself, and step up when you actually add a truck or a tech. That's the ideal shape for a one-truck shop, cheap and simple now, room to grow later, no forklift upgrade when you do.

body.h2: When even Jobber is too much
body.answer: If you book only a few jobs a week and nothing slips, a notebook and calendar still beat any software.
body.html:
Here's the part the software blogs skip. If you're booking a handful of jobs a week and nothing is slipping, you might not need any of this yet. A notebook, your phone calendar, and a simple invoicing app can carry a very small shop a long way. Don't buy software to feel legit. Buy it when manual starts costing you jobs or evenings.

Not sure which side of that line you're on? Read do you need field service software. It's a two-minute gut check that might save you a monthly bill.

And if you're a brand-new shop still finding your feet, lean toward waiting. Your first few months are about proving you can book and finish work, not about picking the perfect platform. Get a dozen happy customers under your belt, see where the manual cracks start showing, then buy the tool that fixes the specific crack. Software bought to solve a problem you can name beats software bought to feel like a real business.

body.h2: Set it up once, then leave it alone
body.answer: Build your quote templates and payment setup once in the first week, then stop fiddling and let the tool run.
body.html:
The mistake solo operators make isn't picking the wrong tool, it's never finishing setup. Spend one evening getting your service list, quote templates, and payment settings dialed in. Then stop tweaking. The tool should fade into the background so you can get back on the tools. If you're spending time inside the software instead of using it to save time, something's backwards.

Want a shortlist beyond Jobber to compare against? The reviews hub has the rest. And if you'd rather hand the setup to someone who's done it a hundred times, talk to a human.

faq.q: Is Jobber really the best for a one-truck shop?
faq.a: For most, yes — it does the solo essentials cleanly and is easy to learn. But 'best' depends on your trade. If payments and marketing matter more to you, Housecall Pro is worth a look too.

faq.q: Do I need software at all with one truck?
faq.a: Not necessarily. If you book a few jobs a week and nothing slips, a notebook and calendar can carry you. Buy software when manual starts costing you jobs or your evenings.

faq.q: How much does Jobber cost for a solo shop?
faq.a: Pricing changes, so check the current numbers in the Jobber review rather than trusting a figure that'll be stale by next quarter. Start on the lowest plan — you can grow into more.
